title: How God Speaks
subtitle: General and special revelation, and how far the heavens can take you without a word.
triageNote: That God has spoken at all is not negotiable. A silent God gives you no gospel, no Bible, and nothing to build a life on, and every position on this page confesses that He has not been silent. What divides faithful churches is the reach of the first kind of speech, the wordless witness of creation and conscience. Whether the stars can prove God, merely point to Him, or say nothing saving at all is a debate inside the family. It has shaped whole traditions. Hold the speaking God tightly. Hold your theory of the stars with an open hand.
question: Christians have always said that God reveals Himself in two ways. General revelation is what God makes known to everyone everywhere through the created world, the moral sense, and the shape of human life. No Bible required. Special revelation is what God makes known by speaking, through prophets and apostles, through Scripture, and finally through His Son. Nobody in this debate denies that both exist. The question is what the first kind can actually do. Can an honest person reason from the world up to God, so that the arguments work and unbelief is a failure of logic. Or does sin so bend the human mind that the world's witness is always received and always suppressed, real enough to leave us without excuse but never enough to save. Or is the whole project of climbing from nature to God a mistake from the first step, because God is known only where He gives Himself, in Jesus Christ.
whyItMatters:
This sounds like a question for philosophers. It is a question for the kitchen table.

You know someone, or you are someone, who stood under a night sky and felt that it meant something, and then wondered whether the feeling was evidence or wishful thinking. You know a believer who lost sleep over the friend who never heard a sermon, and asked what the stars could have told him. You have heard a preacher say the existence of God can be proven, and another say that proofs are a waste of breath, because the heart, not the head, is where the resistance lives. Those three voices are not being careless. They are standing in three old and serious rooms of the one house.

What you decide here sets the terms for almost everything downstream. It decides how you talk to your skeptical neighbor, whether you reach first for an argument, a story, or the person of Christ. It decides what you think is happening inside the scientist who is moved by the elegance of the mathematics and calls it nothing. It decides what you believe about the woman in a village no missionary reached. And it quietly decides how you read the Bible itself. Scripture is special revelation. What you think it was given to do depends on what you think the world had already said.

positions.name: The classical view: nature really argues
positions.inOneLine: General revelation grounds a true natural knowledge of God, so that reason working on the world can establish that He is, and grace then completes what nature begins.
positions.bestCase:
Begin where Paul begins in Romans 1. The invisible attributes of God, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. Clearly perceived. Paul does not say dimly intuited or wished for. He says the world is an argument, and that the argument lands, which is exactly why those who refuse it are without excuse. You cannot be guilty for rejecting evidence that was never really evidence.

Thomas Aquinas built on that conviction in the Summa Theologiae, begun around 1265, with his five ways. Five paths of reasoning from the world we can see, its motion, its causes, its contingency, its degrees of perfection, its order. Back to the One who must stand behind them. He was not replacing faith with logic. He was honoring that God made minds as well as souls, and the God who wrote Scripture also wrote the world, so the two books cannot contradict. My tradition said it formally at the First Vatican Council in 1870: God can be known with certainty from created things by the natural light of human reason. Known with certainty. Not guessed at.

Notice what this view does not claim. Nature does not tell you that God is triune. It does not tell you about the cross, or forgiveness, or your own name being called. Natural knowledge of God is real, and saving knowledge of God is more. That is why special revelation is not optional. Grace does not destroy nature. It perfects it. The arguments clear the ground so the gospel can build the house.

And consider what is lost if I am wrong. If the world's witness does not really reach the mind, then the unbeliever's unbelief is reasonable, and Paul's without excuse becomes a hard saying with nothing under it. If reason cannot get even to the threshold of God, then faith looks, to every watching skeptic, like a leap in the dark. And we have conceded the public square before the conversation starts. I refuse that concession. When Paul stood on the Areopagus in Acts 17 he quoted the Athenians' own poets back to them. Because even pagan poetry had felt its way toward the God in whom we live and move and have our being. The feeling was not wrong. It was unfinished.

positions.name: The Reformed view: revealed, received, suppressed
positions.inOneLine: General revelation is real and constant, but fallen people suppress it, so it leaves everyone without excuse while saving no one. Only Scripture, opened by the Spirit, brings us home.
positions.bestCase:
I agree with my classical friends about the first half of Romans 1 and I beg them to keep reading the verse before it. The wrath of God is revealed against people who suppress the truth in unrighteousness. Suppress. That single word is my whole position. The knowledge gets through, which is why no one has an excuse, and the knowledge gets buried, which is why no one ever reasoned his way to the foot of the cross.

John Calvin, in the 1559 edition of the Institutes, said that God has planted in every human mind a sensus divinitatis, an awareness of divinity. And that the world is a theater of God's glory playing to a full house every day. So I am not the one with the low view of general revelation. I think it is everywhere, relentless, inescapable. In the sky, in the conscience, in the strange human inability to stop worshiping something. But Calvin also said that this seed of religion, in fallen hands, grows crooked. We do not receive the witness neutrally and weigh it like jurors. We take it and bend it into idols. The history of religion is not the history of people following the light of nature up to God. It is the history of people taking that light and making golden calves by it.

This is why I am unmoved when the arguments fail to convert the philosopher. The problem was never in the syllogism. Paul says the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, that the mind set on the flesh is hostile to God. The unbeliever is not an honest calculator missing a premise. He is, as I am apart from grace, a suppressor with a motive. Calvin's image is the one I would leave you with. Scripture is the pair of spectacles. The old man can see the page of creation. The page was always legible. But everything is blurred until the lenses are set on his nose. And even then it is the Spirit who opens the eyes behind the lenses.

So I do not throw away arguments. Herman Bavinck, in his 1908 Princeton lectures on the philosophy of revelation, taught me that every human philosophy lives off borrowed revelation. Pointing that out is good work. But I aim my hope differently. I do not argue people into the kingdom. I bear witness to the Word, because faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.
advocates: R. C. Sproul (with a classical accent)

positions.name: The Barthian view: revelation is Christ
positions.inOneLine: There is no usable natural theology at all. Revelation is not information lying around in the world. It is the event of God giving Himself in Jesus Christ, witnessed by Scripture.
positions.bestCase:
You will understand my severity if you remember the year I learned it. In 1934 the German Christian movement was teaching that God had revealed Himself in nature, in history, and now in the German nation and its leader. Natural theology had become the open door through which an idol walked into the church wearing a uniform. That same year the Confessing Church answered at Barmen, in a declaration I helped draft, that Jesus Christ, as he is attested for us in Holy Scripture, is the one Word of God which we have to hear. And that we reject the false doctrine that the church could and would have to acknowledge as a source of its proclamation other events and powers, figures and truths, as God's revelation. When Emil Brunner, my friend, argued that same year that a point of contact for the gospel remained in natural man, I answered him with a pamphlet. Its entire title was the German word for no.

But do not reduce my position to an emergency measure. It is what I believe about God. Revelation is not a deposit of facts that the universe leaks and clever minds collect. Revelation is an event, a personal act, God unveiling God. And it has a name, Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God, John writes, but the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known. Whoever has seen me, Jesus says, has seen the Father. Long ago God spoke through the prophets, Hebrews begins, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son. Notice that even the prophets were not philosophers of nature. They were addressed. Revelation comes down. It is never climbed up to.

What the natural theologian builds, even with the best intentions, is a god assembled from the world. A first cause, an unmoved mover, a guarantor of the moral order. That god is an idea. Ideas do not forgive sins. Worse, that god is made in the image of the climber, which is why every natural theology ends up baptizing the climber's culture. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is known only where He gives Himself to be known, in the manger, on the cross, out of the tomb. And the Bible is holy precisely as the witness that points there, the way the Baptist's long finger points in Grünewald's altarpiece.

As for the heavens declaring the glory of God, I believe Psalm 19 with all my heart, read in order. The man who wrote that the skies pour forth speech is the man who already stood inside the covenant. He could finish the psalm with the law of the Lord reviving the soul. Creation sings to those whom the Word has given ears. It hands no ladder to those still climbing.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Contested ground, claimed by the classical and Reformed views alike
biblicalEvidence.summary: God's eternal power and divine nature have been clearly perceived in the things that have been made, so that all people are without excuse. And yet this truth is suppressed in unrighteousness and ends in idolatry. The whole debate lives inside these four verses.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the Barthian view, because Paul plainly says that something of God is known and perceived from creation by people outside the covenant. That is at least a real general revelation.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The classical view underlines clearly perceived and builds natural theology on it. The Reformed view underlines suppress and argues the perception is real but never neutrally received. Sufficient for guilt and not for salvation. The Barthian view replies that Paul is describing revelation refused, a wrath-revealing situation. Nothing in the passage suggests anyone can reason from the world to the true God, only that everyone is accountable to Him.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The classical view, with the turn at verse 7 claimed by everyone
biblicalEvidence.summary: The heavens declare the glory of God, day to day pours out speech, there is no speech, nor are there words, yet their voice goes out through all the earth. Then the psalm turns: the law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul. Creation speaks. And the written word does what creation cannot.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that makes general revelation either everything or nothing, because the psalm holds both witnesses together and assigns soul-reviving power only to the second.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The classical view hears verses 1 to 6 as proof that the world genuinely communicates God to all people. The Reformed view notes that the psalmist is a covenant believer who hears the skies rightly because he already has the law, and that revival of the soul belongs to the word alone. The Barthian view reads the whole psalm as doxology from inside faith, not as an argument addressed to those outside it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul in Athens reasons with pagan philosophers and quotes their own poets, Epimenides and Aratus, with approval. He argues from creation and providence toward the God who now commands all people everywhere to repent. The resurrection is the proof.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the Barthian view. Paul treats pagan religious groping, that they would feel their way toward him and find him, as something to build on rather than only to demolish.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The classical view sees here the charter for natural theology in evangelism, common ground honestly used. The Reformed view observes that Paul calls the city given over to idols, names their worship ignorance, and converts almost no one by the argument. The speech ends in mockery and a few believers, which fits a witness that condemns and prepares more than it persuades. The Barthian view stresses that Paul does not finish at the unknown god but at Jesus and the resurrection. That is where revelation actually happens.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, a baseline text for general revelation
biblicalEvidence.summary: At Lystra Paul says God did not leave himself without witness, for he gave rains and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness. Providence itself, the ordinary kindness of the harvest, is testimony.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Mildly hard for the Barthian view, since the witness here is given to nations walking in their own ways, outside the covenant. And it is called a witness.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The classical and Reformed views both claim this comfortably, differing only on what the witness achieves. The Barthian view grants a testimony of kindness that leaves humanity accountable, while denying it amounts to a knowledge of God that theology could build on. Paul's actual sermon at Lystra is an urgent call to turn from these vain things to the living God.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The classical view, with strong Reformed use
biblicalEvidence.summary: Gentiles who do not have the law sometimes do what the law requires, showing that the work of the law is written on their hearts. Their conscience bears witness, their thoughts accusing or even excusing them. Conscience is a second channel of general revelation alongside the stars.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any account that says fallen people retain no true moral knowledge at all, since Paul says the law's work is written on pagan hearts and sometimes done.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The classical view takes this as the foundation of natural law, a shared moral grammar that argument can appeal to. The Reformed view agrees the writing is real but adds that conscience is also fallen, accusing and excusing unevenly. A witness for the prosecution more than a ladder to God. The Barthian view reads it within Paul's courtroom argument that every mouth will be stopped, evidence of accountability, not a doctrine of natural moral ascent.

biblicalEvidence.summary: In the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, and it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe. Whatever the world's wisdom achieved, it did not arrive at the knowledge of God. Salvation came another way.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the classical view, because Paul seems to render a verdict on the project of reasoning up to God: the world did not know God through wisdom.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The classical view answers that Paul is judging the pride and idolatry of Greek wisdom, not the validity of reasoning from creation. Paul himself uses that reasoning in Romans 1 and Acts 17, and knowing God savingly was never what natural theology claimed to deliver. The Reformed view hears its own doctrine stated plainly. The Barthian view hears the cross declared as the one place God is known. And the preached word as the means.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son. Revelation is speech, it is historical, it is progressive. Its final form is a person.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any account that treats revelation primarily as information available in nature, since the text frames revelation as God speaking, in acts of address, climaxing in Christ.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The classical and Reformed views agree gladly that special revelation climaxes in the Son. They simply deny that this cancels the world's wordless witness, since the same chapter says the Son upholds the universe by the word of his power. The Barthian view takes the verse as the architecture of all theology: God has spoken in his Son, and every other claimed revelation must be measured there.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The Reformed view, with full Barthian agreement
biblicalEvidence.summary: How are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard, and how are they to hear without someone preaching. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. Whatever the stars say, saving faith arrives by the sent word.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any hope that general revelation alone might save, since Paul ties faith to hearing the word of Christ preached.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The classical view agrees entirely, which is worth noticing: Vatican I affirmed natural knowledge of God's existence, not natural salvation. The Reformed view finds here the reason missions exist and the reason arguments are never enough. The Barthian view adds that this is why the church's one task is proclamation, bearing witness to the Word who has already spoken.

weighing:
Here is my own judgment, offered the way I would offer it across a table, tentatively and with my Bible open.

I cannot get around Romans 1, in both of its directions. Paul says the world's witness is clearly perceived. That means the night sky is not a private mood, it is testimony, and the person who feels addressed by it is feeling something true. Paul also says the testimony is suppressed. That matches everything I have seen in twenty years of conversations with people who had every argument answered and still did not come. The resistance was never really in the head. So I find myself living in the Reformed room of this house. The windows are open toward the other two.

Toward the classical room, because I have watched arguments matter. Not save, but matter. A good argument can dismantle the false confidence that faith is for the unintelligent. And that demolition is real ministry. The classical tradition is right that the God of the Bible is not embarrassed by reason, and right that without excuse must mean the evidence really reaches people. Toward the Barthian room, because Barth saw something in 1934 that I do not want to forget. Every generation is tempted to find God's voice in its own nation, its own moment, its own causes. And a church without his severity will eventually bless its own reflection and call it revelation. The test of every claimed word from God is the Word made flesh.

If you press me to one sentence, it is this. The heavens preach, and the sermon is true, and no one was ever saved by the stars, because the stars do not know your name, and the gospel is the news that Someone does. Hold general revelation high enough to honor the witness, and not so high that you stop sending preachers.
charitableDisagreement:
Each of these rooms is guarding a treasure. The classical view is guarding the public truthfulness of the faith, the conviction that Christianity does not ask anyone to put out his eyes. And that the God who made reason is not threatened by it. The Reformed view is guarding the depth of sin and the freeness of grace, the honest observation that conversion is a rescue, not a conclusion. The Barthian view is guarding the first commandment. The church's vulnerability to idols that arrive speaking the language of nature, common sense, and the times. You can fail by dismissing any of them. Churches have.

Is it a hill to die on. That God has revealed Himself, in the world He made and supremely in the Son He sent, yes. That is the faith itself. But the reach of natural theology, whether the arguments establish, gesture, or mislead, is a debate among people who confess the same Lord. They read the same Romans 1 and want the same neighbor saved. Aquinas, Calvin, and Barth are not enemies. They are three sentries posted at three different gates. The city has needed all three. Argue your post with conviction. Honor the other gates. And whatever you decide about the stars, keep telling people about the Son, because on that, all three sentries agree.

relatedDebates.note: Special revelation reaches us as a written book. The next question is how the breath of God became human words. The models of inspiration, from dictation to encounter, are the natural continuation of this doctrine, and your view of revelation quietly shapes which model feels like home.

relatedDebates.topic: The fate of those who never hear
relatedDebates.note: If general revelation leaves everyone without excuse but saves no one, the question of the unevangelized becomes acute. Some hold God judges according to the light received. Some that the light received is precisely what condemns. Some that God gets special revelation to everyone He is drawing. Every answer leans on a doctrine of revelation. That is why this page comes first.

The long argument between classical apologetics, evidentialism, and presuppositionalism is downstream of this page. Whether you reason to God from shared ground or argue that there is no neutral ground at all depends on what you believe sin did to the mind that weighs the evidence.
